_meta.description: The argument the whole dashboard rests on, stated plainly — including the parts that have not gone our way. Reviewed whenever the Scoreboard's forward record materially changes.

headline: Own the gates, not the brands — knowing they are contested, and that owning them is leverage on the AI trade rather than shelter from it.

sections.b: Across AI hardware, value concentrates at the stages nobody can easily replicate. The end-products are contested and crowded — merchant GPUs against custom ASICs, this humanoid against that one, one pair of glasses against another — and competition there grinds margin away. But every contender flows through the same narrow gates: ASML's lithography, TSMC's leading edge and CoWoS packaging, HBM from a handful of suppliers, Ajinomoto's insulating film, VAT's vacuum valves. Own the gate and you get paid regardless of which brand wins.

A chokepoint is not the same as a large company. The test is mechanical: if this supplier stopped tomorrow, how long until someone else could do it, and at what cost? Where the honest answer runs to years and billions — a decade and $100B+ to replicate a leading-edge fab, decades of optical know-how inside a single German firm — pricing power follows without needing to forecast demand correctly. That is what conviction-3 means here, and why only 25 of 235 names carry it.

sections.k: What has not gone our way
sections.b: Three things, stated plainly. It is leverage, not safety. Since the conviction ranking was set on 30 May, the chokepoint basket has underperformed semis — irreplaceable assets get bid hardest and de-rate hardest, so this is the theme's risk in its most concentrated form, not a hiding place. Chokepoints are contested. HBM4 became the first triple-qualified memory generation, diluting per-supplier power, and we cut Micron's rating for it; the FCC's draft transceiver ban would manufacture a chokepoint for Western optics and destroy one for InnoLight, purely by rule. Qualification and policy contest these positions as much as technology does. The froth lens is unproven. It was written on 1 August and has no meaningful record — the Scoreboard publishes it as it accumulates rather than claiming it later.

If the conviction-3 basket keeps losing to semis over a rolling six months while hyperscaler capex guidance holds, the premise is wrong: value would be accruing to the deployers and model owners rather than the suppliers, and this map is looking in the wrong place. The second falsifier is sustained inference-price deflation with flat token volume, which breaks the demand spine under every vertical at once.

sections.k: How the ratings are actually used
sections.b: Conviction measures replaceability, never cheapness. A conviction-3 name can be a terrible purchase at the wrong price. The froth lens carries valuation — the two are read together and never merged into one score. A drawdown means opposite things depending on where it starts: more than 15% off the high in an insulated chokepoint is an entry window; the same fall in a high-froth name is just air leaving a price that was never anchored. Everything carries a date, because a judgment without one is a guess.

An external view worth holding against this map, from an investor inventory supplied 2026-08-08. Avoid semiconductors outright on the argument that Chinese competitiveness and lower production cost erode the pricing power the whole thesis rests on — a direct attack on the premise, not a quibble with a name. GPU rental prices are going up, not down, which contradicts the inference-price-deflation signal the Froth Monitor treats as a froth marker; if rental economics are improving, the GPU-renter layer we flag as high-froth is mispriced in our direction, not theirs. Hyperscalers at roughly 10x EV/sales are vulnerable to step-function capex — which is the demand spine of every vertical here. We do not adopt these views, but the first would break the thesis and the second contradicts a live signal, so they are recorded rather than filed away.
